title: Radiographic Techniques I: Skeletal and Chest
description: Positioning principles and standard projections of the chest, upper and lower limbs, spine, pelvis and skull, with image evaluation criteria.

topics.title: Principles of Positioning and Projection Terminology
topics.summary: Projection terms, centring, collimation, the two-views rule and patient care.

notes.b: A projection describes the path of the central ray: posteroanterior (PA — beam enters posterior, exits anterior, receptor in front), anteroposterior (AP), lateral (named by the side nearest the receptor, e.g. right lateral), oblique, and axial (angled along the long axis). Positions describe the patient: erect, supine, prone, decubitus (lying with a horizontal beam). The central ray is centred on a stated anatomical point and the beam is collimated to the area of interest, which reduces dose and scatter. Anatomical side markers (R/L) must be placed within the field before exposure.
k: Lateral named by side nearest receptor
Always use R/L markers and collimate

notes.b: The 'rule of two' — at least two views at right angles (usually AP/PA and lateral) — is standard for skeletal trauma, as a fracture or dislocation may be invisible on a single view; include the joints above and below a long-bone fracture. Justification (every exposure must benefit the patient) and optimisation (ALARA — as low as reasonably achievable) apply. Confirm patient identity and pregnancy status in women of reproductive age (the '28-day rule' or '10-day rule' for high-dose pelvic examinations). Communicate clearly, immobilise gently, and use lead shielding where it does not obscure anatomy.

Enters the back and exits the front

Decubitus views use a horizontal beam to show fluid levels or free air.

topics.title: Chest and Abdomen Radiography
topics.summary: PA and lateral chest, AP supine chest, abdomen views, and image quality criteria.

notes.b: The standard chest radiograph is an erect PA taken on full inspiration at about 180 cm source-to-image distance (SID); the PA projection minimises magnification of the heart and allows the scapulae to be rotated out of the lung fields (hands on hips, shoulders forward). Quality criteria: correct identification; adequate inspiration (about 6 anterior or 10 posterior ribs above the diaphragm); no rotation (medial ends of clavicles equidistant from the spinous processes); adequate penetration (vertebral bodies just visible through the heart); whole lung fields including costophrenic angles. AP supine chest films (ill patients) magnify the heart, so cardiac size cannot be reliably assessed. A cardiothoracic ratio > 0.5 on a PA film suggests cardiomegaly.
k: Erect PA at 180 cm, full inspiration

notes.b: The standard abdominal radiograph is AP supine, covering from the diaphragm to the symphysis pubis (to include the kidneys, ureters and bladder — 'KUB'). Pneumoperitoneum (perforated viscus) is best shown by an erect chest radiograph (free gas under the diaphragm) — the patient should be upright for 10 minutes if possible — or a left lateral decubitus abdomen. Intestinal obstruction shows dilated loops and, on erect or decubitus films, air–fluid levels. The abdomen is exposed on arrested expiration.
k: AP supine abdomen: diaphragm to symphysis
Left lateral decubitus for free air

topics.title: Upper Limb and Shoulder
topics.summary: Hand, wrist, scaphoid, elbow, shoulder and clavicle projections.

notes.b: Hand: dorsipalmar (PA) and dorsipalmar oblique; a lateral is added for foreign bodies or metacarpal fracture displacement. Wrist: PA and lateral with the forearm in contact with the receptor. Scaphoid series: PA with ulnar deviation (elongates the scaphoid), oblique views and a lateral; if clinical suspicion persists with normal films, the patient is immobilised and re-imaged at 10–14 days or has MRI/CT, because initial films may miss the fracture and non-union or avascular necrosis can follow. A lateral wrist shows the Colles' (dorsal) and Smith's (volar) fracture displacement.
k: Scaphoid: PA with ulnar deviation + obliques
Occult scaphoid fracture: repeat at 10–14 days or MRI

notes.b: Elbow: AP with the elbow extended and lateral with 90° flexion; the lateral shows the fat pads — a visible posterior fat pad ('sail sign') indicates an effusion and possible occult fracture (e.g. radial head in adults, supracondylar in children). Shoulder: AP (or true AP/Grashey), plus an axial (supero-inferior) or 'Y' scapular lateral view to confirm anterior or posterior dislocation; posterior dislocation may give a 'light bulb' humeral head on the AP. Clavicle: PA/AP and an angled (cranial) view.
k: Shoulder dislocation: axial or Y view

topics.title: Lower Limb and Pelvis
topics.summary: Foot, ankle, knee, hip and pelvis projections with key trauma considerations.

notes.b: Foot: dorsiplantar and dorsiplantar oblique (lateral for foreign bodies or Lisfranc injuries). Ankle: AP (or 'mortise' view with about 15–20° internal rotation to show the joint space evenly) and lateral. Clinical decision rules (Ottawa ankle rules) reduce unnecessary imaging. Knee: AP and lateral; a horizontal-beam lateral shows a lipohaemarthrosis (fat–fluid level), indicating an intra-articular fracture such as a tibial plateau fracture. Skyline (tangential) view shows the patellofemoral joint. Weight-bearing AP views assess joint-space narrowing in osteoarthritis.

Pelvis: AP with the legs internally rotated about 15–20° (brings the femoral necks parallel to the receptor, showing them in full length). Hip: AP and a lateral (horizontal-beam 'cross-table' lateral in suspected neck-of-femur fracture — do not move the leg into a frog-leg position if a fracture is suspected). Signs of femoral neck fracture: disruption of Shenton's line, shortening and external rotation of the leg. Pelvic fractures may cause major haemorrhage; handle trauma patients with minimal movement.
k: Suspected NOF fracture: cross-table lateral (no frog-leg)

topics.title: Spine and Skull
topics.summary: Cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine projections, trauma precautions and skull and sinus views.

notes.b: Cervical spine trauma series: lateral (must show C7/T1 junction — use a 'swimmer's' view or traction on the arms if needed), AP, and open-mouth odontoid (peg) view; CT is now preferred for significant trauma. The patient's neck is immobilised (collar, blocks) until injury is excluded; do not remove the collar or move the head. Thoracic spine: AP and lateral. Lumbar spine: AP and lateral (obliques show the pars interarticularis — the 'Scotty dog' neck in spondylolysis). Lumbar spine radiographs carry a relatively high gonadal dose and are not routinely indicated for simple back pain without red flags.
k: Keep collar on until injury excluded

notes.b: Skull radiography has largely been replaced by CT for head injury. Standard skull projections include occipitofrontal (OF/PA with 15–20° caudal angulation — Caldwell), fronto-occipital 30° (Towne's — for the occiput), and lateral. The occipitomental (OM, Waters') view at 45° shows the maxillary sinuses and facial bones (including orbital floor 'blow-out' and zygomatic fractures); a horizontal beam shows fluid levels. The orbitomeatal baseline (outer canthus to external auditory meatus) is the reference line for skull positioning.
k: CT has replaced skull X-ray for head injury
OM (Waters'): facial bones and maxillary sinuses
